newsitem.title: UK: Italian debt rally fails to spark new fund buying.
newsitem.headline: Italian debt rally fails to spark new fund buying.

text.p: A scorching rally in Italian bonds is failing to ignite interest among London-based fund managers, who are reluctant to make bigger bets either for or against European Monetary Union (EMU).
The gap between yields on Italian and German government bonds has narrowed rapidly in recent days -- hitting a record low of 111 basis points.
But fund managers are looking outside Europe for fixed-interest investment, saying they will ride current positions rather than take on more risk in a politically-driven market.

"It is very difficult to take a confident bet on euro issues right now. From an institutional investor's point of view, I don't think we can second guess on politics," said Rhys Herbert fixed income strategist at Prudential Portfolio Management, who finds US and British debt markets more attractive and safe bets now.
"I think it is tough right now to take a strong position on any number of European markets," he said.

"I don't think that a lot of fund managers have an aggressive convergence bet on now, which is why you see an absence of selling pressure," said Jonathan Cunliffe, fixed-income specialist at fund manager Lombard Odier.

Betting that Italian and German yields will gravitate towards one another in the runup to EMU has been a popular and winning play in fixed income markets, with BTP/Bund spreads narrowing by more than 40 basis points in recent weeks.

Opinion is sharply split on the fate of convergence bets from here, but most fund managers agreed that volatility and the high level of unpredictability in the EMU process make them more likely to sit on the sidelines than wade into the fray.

Stewart Cowley, head of fixed income at Hill Samuel Asset Management, is bullish on Italian Bonds, seeing a further narrowing of the spread with Bunds to 80 basis points, but he is cautious about committing himself to the bet.
"A trader would go for it, if you are an investor its not worth it," Cowley, who controls an 8 billion stg portfolio, said.
He is holding on to his slightly overweight position in Italian government debt, "But we are taking it as a longer term trade, we will take the volatility."

He sees EMU coming in on time and tight, with a political deal that allows Italy to come in two years late. This implies a hard euro, and Cowley thinks the glow from this will spread to Italian government debt.
One concern for Cowley is that, according to Hill Samuel's models, the lira is overvalued, a fact he thinks won't be recognised until the dust around EMU has settled.

"The main risk (on a convergence trade) is, yes, you can squeeze out the last part but you will get stuffed on the currency devaluation when the lira comes back to some sort of reasonable levels against the mark."

Cunliffe also has a BTP/Bund spread target of 80 basis points by the end of the year, "if Bunds stay range-bound it would be consistent with 10-year yields down at around 6.4-6.5 percent in Italy, which is not unreasonable," he said.

He thinks that BTPs will be supported by strong liquidity in the domestic market and, unlike Cowley, thinks that some fund mangers may be tempted to load up now to ride the Bund spread down to 80 basis points.
"If you look at a range-bound Bund and a U.S. bond market with a slightly higher bias, there are not a lot of other opportunities around to make money."
Herbert, preferring to play in U.S. and British fixed income markets, is negative on BTPs, setting a target of about 125 basis points for the spread with Bunds.
"On a historic basis they look overvalued and risk premiums look low, even if we factor in quite low inflation rates."
"Clearly what the market is betting on is Italy in or close to EMU by 1999 or not long after that," Herbert said.
"They are also betting on Italian yields falling to German levels. Yields may in fact converge, but at a higher level than German yields are currently."
